interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle relationships between entities in a NoSQL data model?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back gently on the framing that NoSQL 'can't do relationships' — it just models them with two techniques instead of a join: embedding, nesting related data directly inside a document, and referencing, storing an ID and looking it up separately. The skill is picking the right one per relationship, not per database.

For a one-to-few relationship that rarely changes and is always read with its parent — an order's line items — I'd embed them directly in the order document. For a one-to-many or many-to-many relationship, or one where the related data changes independently — a post's author, or tags on posts — I'd reference by ID instead, accepting an extra application-side lookup rather than duplicating data that would need to be kept in sync everywhere it's copied.

For many-to-many specifically, I'd use a join collection storing ID pairs, mirroring a relational join table, and resolve it with two lookups in application code.

**Testing:** whether you know the two real techniques and can choose per relationship instead of assuming NoSQL simply can't model relationships.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Modeling relationships in NoSQL

interviewQuestions.question: The embedded list of line-items keeps growing unbounded — is embedding still right?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No — an unbounded, growing list is a sign the relationship isn't actually one-to-few anymore, and that's exactly the condition under which embedding stops being the right technique. Most document stores also have a hard document size limit, and even well below that limit, every read and write to the parent now moves more data than necessary as the list keeps growing.

I'd switch that specific relationship to referencing: move the growing list into its own collection with a reference back to the parent order, while leaving any other genuinely small, stable relationships on the same entity embedded. This decision is made per relationship, not as an all-or-nothing choice for the whole entity.

I'd also treat unbounded growth as a signal to revisit early — waiting until a document hits its size limit in production is a worse time to make this change than catching it as a design smell first.

**Testing:** whether you'll recognize embedding has stopped fitting the data's actual shape and change course, instead of forcing the original design to keep working.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: When embedding stops working

interviewQuestions.question: How would you enforce something like a foreign-key constraint here, since the database won't do it for you?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Since most NoSQL databases don't enforce referential integrity natively, I'd treat it as an explicit application responsibility rather than assume the database has it covered. At write time, I'd validate that a referenced ID actually exists before saving the reference, rather than saving it blind and discovering a dangling reference later.

For deletions, I'd decide deliberately between two options: cascade the deletion to dependents in application code when the relationship genuinely requires it, or leave the reference in place and handle a missing lookup gracefully on read — returning a placeholder rather than letting the request error out unexpectedly.

I'd name this directly as a real cost of referencing without native constraints: a guarantee a relational foreign key gives for free now has to be built, tested, and maintained by hand in the application layer.

**Testing:** whether you understand that referencing shifts a real responsibility to the application, and can name concrete mechanisms for handling it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Enforcing referential integrity
